A.explanation: $1.6 \text{ mA} = 1.6 \times 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{A} = 1600 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$, which matches the analogue reading.

B.explanation: $160 \text{ } \mu\text{A} = 0.16 \text{ mA}$, which is ten times smaller than the needle position near $1.6 \text{ mA}$.

C.explanation: $16.0 \text{ mA}$ is ten times larger than the reading and would point beyond the $15 \text{ mA}$ end of the scale.

D.explanation: $1.60 \text{ A} = 1600 \text{ mA}$, which is one thousand times larger than the $1.6 \text{ mA}$ reading.

hints: Look at the analogue scale labelled milliamperes (mA) - the needle is between 0 and 5, just past 1, about $1.6 \text{ mA}$.
Recall the prefix conversions for current: $1 \text{ mA} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$ and $1 \text{ A} = 1000 \text{ mA}$.
Convert $1.6 \text{ mA}$ into $\mu\text{A}$ and into A, then compare the size of each display reading with the needle position.
walkthrough: Read the analogue dial: the scale is in $\text{milliamperes (mA)}$ from 0 to 15, and the needle points to about $1.6 \text{ mA}$.
State the prefix rule: milli means $10^{-3}$ and micro means $10^{-6}$, so $1 \text{ mA} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$.
Check the other units: $1.6 \text{ mA} = 0.0016 \text{ A}$, so $1.60 \text{ A}$ and $16.0 \text{ mA}$ are far too large.
Therefore the matching digital display is $1600$ with units $\mu\text{A}$. This is option A.
